articles.title: OpenAI Industrial Espionage Trial Exposes Corporate Eavesdropping Vulnerabilities
articles.content: LivestreamMenuA San Francisco federal judge set a Jan. 20 trial for Saudi national and former OpenAI engineering lead Abdulrahman Alfozan.Alfozan is accused of installing a recording device in an OpenAI conference room when he worked for the artificial intelligence company.Alfozan's attorney wants to use an AI tool created by an OpenAI competitor to review evidence. Prosecutors are concerned about exposing proprietary OpenAI data if that is allowed.Photo of Abdulrahman Alfozan checking a recording device in OpenAI's office in San Francisco, according to the Department of Justice.Courtesy: U.S. Department of JusticeA federal judge on Tuesday set Jan. 20 for the start of the trial for Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, who is accused of planting a recording device in an OpenAI conference room when he worked for the artificial intelligence company as an engineering lead. If the trial starts on that date in U.S. District Court in San Francisco, it would be after an unusually short lag since Alfozan's arrest in October. Federal criminal cases, as a rule, do not go to trial so quickly. But Alfozan's attorney, David Rizk, sought the speedy trial after complaining at a court hearing that prosecutors have been slow in turning over evidence in the case. Rizk also said prosecutors have not given him any evidence that Alfozan engaged in espionage, after they argued successfully last month that he should be detained without bail, and after saying his alleged bugging "could pose a danger to the national security of the United States." Among other things, prosecutors had noted that Alfozan is a venture partner at Saudi venture firm Raed Ventures alongside a member of the Saudi royal family, Prince Khalid bin Bader Al Saud. Alfozan, who has pleaded not guilty in the case, is charged with one count of intercepting oral communications. He faces a maximum of five years in prison if he is convicted. Prosecutors have said Alfozan was arrested after staff at OpenAI found a recording device wrapped in toilet paper and installed in the back of a television in the conference room at its San Francisco headquarters in September. A surveillance camera captured Alfozan looking at the gadget in the room. Assistant U.S. Attorney Nick Parker told Judge Vince Chhabria on Tuesday that government investigators have been locked out of Alfozan's phone, but they have also collected one other phone, a tablet, and two laptops. Prosecutors also obtained 160 hours of recordings from meetings in a conference room. The recording device itself is encrypted, but if data was backed up to another device, investigators would have been able to obtain it, Parker said. Chhabria told prosecutors that they must turn over all reports the FBI has created to Alfozan's attorney by Nov. 24, and that they must also move quickly to give the defense other evidence for use at trial. "We need to make sure that you get whatever discovery you're entitled to promptly," Chhabria told Rizk. OpenAI, which fired Alfozan after his arrest, has said it lacked proof of him taking source code or customer data. Chhabria also told Parker he wants to see, within seven days, any evidence that might exist showing Alfozan carrying out economic espionage, stealing trade secrets or acting as an unregistered foreign agent. Parker said he was not aware of any such evidence at this time. "At this point, I'm not suggesting the defendant stole anything," Parker said. The prosecutor told the judge that his team had a "serious concern" about Rizk's plans to review evidence turned over to the defense with an AI tool that competes with OpenAI. Parker noted that among the seized evidence is a laptop that might have proprietary OpenAI data. Chhabria replied, "I'm a lot less concerned about that than you are." The judge ordered Parker to submit a motion by Friday explaining why the defense's use of a competing AI to analyze evidence might be a problem. Rizk told CNBC he intends to use Anthropic's Claude. Anthropic, which aims to go public on Nasdaq this week, was founded by OpenAI employees. — CNBC's Dan Mangan contributed to this report. articles.title: Intelligence Chiefs Point to Algorithmic Surges in Infrastructure Outages
articles.content: Director of National Intelligence offers explanation for tech outages by Tara Suter - 11/17/26 7:41 PM ET Link copied - 11/17/26 7:41 PM ET Link copied NOW PLAYING Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton pushed back Tuesday on public speculation surrounding recent tech outages, attributing many to system upgrades as opposed to cyberattacks. “Let me tell you what this is not, as far as we can tell … this is not a cyberattack, and this is not a coordinated effort by a nation state. We’ve looked very closely,” Clayton told CNBC. “What I think is going on here, and I think there’s both a good news aspect to this and an aspect that we need to be clear-eyed about, is many people are patching their systems,” he added. “They know that they’re legacy systems, have vulnerabilities, they’re outdated … it is time for an upgrade across our digital infrastructure.” Clayton’s comments came as high-profile tech outages hit multiple industries within the last week — impacting flights, banking systems, email and beyond — which raised alarm bells nationwide surrounding the potential for large-scale cybersecurity breaches. And Trump administration officials were left to answer for them. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said super intelligence (SI) — the administration’s preferred term for artificial intelligence — may be the cause of the recent tech outages, citing a discussion with an unidentified member of the tech industry. “I started talking to the tech industry,” Mullin told Fox News on Monday, adding he talked to a person in tech that thought “that it’s the SI, he said, because these programs aren’t designed to work as fast as SI is.” “When they put in a program that’s able to write codes and it goes in, it self-fixes itself,” Mullin continued. “It’s like doing a change order on a house. When you change one thing in a house, everything else starts changing, that’s a ripple effect. And it causes a system to be overran that weren’t designed to run as fast as the SI technology is today.” Clayton echoed Mullin’s point Tuesday, signaling that tech infrastructure “upgrades” — including the integration of AI — may have led to the recent issues. Microsoft users across the globe last Thursday experienced widespread outages affecting platforms including Outlook and Teams. The problem lasted for about a day and was “introduced by an issue during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the company said after restoring the platforms. The day after, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop, stretching on for more than four hours. Officials initially linked the incident to an overload of data on routers, with Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy later saying a contractor’s telecommunications line switch caused the issue that sparked the stoppage. articles.title: California Freeway Ban Halts Waymo Autonomous Trucking Ambitions
articles.content: Sign up now: Get ST's newsletters delivered to your inbox The ban applies to both testing and operating of Waymo vehicles on freeways. PHOTO: ARIANA GOMEZ/NYTIMES Published Nov 18, 2026, 07:21 AM Updated Nov 18, 2026, 08:48 AM Set as preferred source Listen Summarise California banned Waymo driverless cars from state freeways after incidents in construction zones and with Highway Patrol vehicles. The DMV said the vehicles pose an “imminent hazard” to public safety. Waymo said it has “temporarily restricted freeway operations across our other operating markets” to review performance. It said the California incidents caused no injuries or collisions. The ban covers both operating and testing on freeways. It will stay until Waymo shows “effective corrective actions” to fix the problems. AI generated SAN FRANCISCO - The robotaxi company Waymo said it temporarily suspended all rides on freeways in its autonomous vehicles after California banned the vehicles from its state freeways after recent traffic incidents. The California Department of Motor Vehicles issued the ban on Nov 11 after two incidents on California freeways, including one where three of Waymo’s driverless vehicles drove into a construction zone, department spokesperson Jonathan Groveman said in a statement. A Waymo spokesperson wrote in an e-mail that the company has “temporarily restricted commercial freeway rides in all markets where we operate that service”, though it is “continuing freeway testing with trained autonomous specialists behind the wheel”. Waymo’s autonomous vehicles have expanded onto freeways in the San Francisco Bay Area, Los Angeles, Phoenix, Miami and Austin, according to the company. The construction zone incident occurred on Nov 5 and the second incident, which involved California Highway Patrol vehicles, occurred the next day on a highway in San Francisco, according to Groveman. Video of the Nov 6 incident circulated widely on social media last week. In the footage, a Waymo vehicle can be seen trying to bypass California Highway Patrol vehicles conducting a traffic break. “The Department determined that Waymo’s driverless freeway operations pose an imminent hazard to public safety due to recurring incursions by its vehicles into active construction zones where construction workers, vehicles and equipment are present,” Groveman said. Groveman added that “similar incidents” previously occurred on May 18. The Waymo spokesperson said the “recent freeway construction zone encounters on US 101 in California” did not “involve any injuries or collisions”. Waymo continues to operate the vehicles as normal on California surface streets , according to the company. California’s restrictions bar Waymo from both operating and testing its driverless vehicles on California freeways, according to Groveman. He said the restrictions will remain in effect until “Waymo demonstrates to the Department that it has taken effective corrective actions to address the deficiencies that precipitated the restrictions”. articles.content: Jensen Huang breaks silence on resignation, says he’d be ‘honored’ to return as Nvidia’s CEO by Miranda Nazzaro - 11/17/26 11:56 AM ET Link copied - 11/17/26 11:56 AM ET Link copied NOW PLAYING Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang broke his silence on Tuesday following his resignation from the company, stating he would be “honored” to return to the role should the company’s Board of Directors support the move. In a statement obtained by The Hill, Huang said he saw an “outpouring of calls” from some Nvidia staff, investors, business partners and customers for him to return as CEO, just days after he resigned from the role amid a national security scandal. “Many continue to reach out to me directly as the company navigates complex technology, market, competitive, and geopolitical dynamics. NVIDIA is a once-in-a-generation company,” Huang wrote. “If the Board of Directors decides that my return is in the best interest of our shareholders, our employees, the company, and America, I would be honored to answer these calls and return as CEO.” A source familiar told The Hill on Monday Nvidia’s Board of Directors is not weighing Huang’s return. Huang resigned days after admitting to an extramarital affair, and reports suggest it was with executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials suspected was a spy for China. The allegations sparked a flood of scrutiny of the longtime CEO, including an independent investigation by Nvidia’s Board of Directors. Alice Huang is a former executive of the Singaporean data center and cloud computing firm Megaspeed, which is under investigation over allegations it smuggled Nvidia’s AI chips into China despite chip export controls. Jensen Huang said on Tuesday he “did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at Nvidia and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life.” “I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board’s independent investigation,” he wrote. Shortly after his resignation, petitions circulated calling for his return, while President Trump said on Monday he “certainly wouldn’t mind” if Huang returned as CEO. “I think he learned a big lesson,” Trump said. “I guess maybe one lesson more important than another, but I would certainly not mind seeing that.” The Financial Times reported over the weekend he is discussed a comeback with allies in Silicon Valley. Several tech executives signed an open letter calling for his reinstatement, including SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. The executives argued Huang should be brought back while an independent investigation is completed. The open letter, which has more than 170,000 signatories, asked the board to “provide compelling evidence that [Huang’s] removal is in Nvidia’s best interests,” and stated the former CEO “deserves due process, not mob justice.” Tags Donald Trump Elon Musk Jensen Huang NVIDIA Travis Kalanick Trump administration Copyright 2026 Nexstar Media Inc. articles.title: Breach at Identity Vendor Exposes Thousands of Uber Driver Licenses
articles.content: Ride-hailing biz says stolen credentials allowed crooks to help themselves to driver's license data Carly Page Carly Page Published tue 17 Nov 2026 // 16:15 UTC Make us preferred on Google GPU giants throw HPC users some tasty crumbs 3 hours ago China’s grip on Top500 remains uncontested as US chases AI-HPC fusion 1 day ago US allies deepen deal to guard AI supply chains against 'hostile actors' (cough, China, cough) 1 day ago Marvell and Penguin Solutions aim to end the RAMpocalypse with photonic memory fabric 1 day ago Elon Musk leads Silicon Valley's campaign to put Jensen Huang back in charge at Nvidia 1 day ago Uber has confirmed that nearly 150,000 people had their personal information compromised after hackers broke into one of its AI suppliers. A filing with Oregon's attorney general puts the number of victims at 149,346. Among the data the crooks got their hands on were images of drivers' licenses and information extracted from them, including names, home addresses, dates of birth, and license numbers. Uber doesn't name the supplier in its filings with US state attorneys general, but told TechCrunch it was Fireworks AI, the inference outfit whose security woes we covered last week . According to a breach notification filed with Iowa's attorney general, Fireworks alerted Uber to the intrusion on October 9. Uber cut off the supplier's access to its data and, four days later, established that the attackers had accessed drivers' personal information on October 7. Uber had set up a dedicated cloud storage environment for the AI biz, complete with security monitoring overseen by its own cloud security team. Unfortunately for Uber and its drivers, the crooks were using legitimate credentials, so none of the alarms went off. The ride-hailing firm says those credentials couldn't be used to access its other systems, and says it has since revoked or changed the credentials associated with the supplier. Uber hasn't said why it handed images of thousands of driver's licenses to an AI inference outfit. The Register has put that question to both companies, and asked Uber if any drivers outside the US had their data exposed. Fireworks, which provides infrastructure for developers to run and fine-tune AI models, had a particularly miserable October. The company first disclosed a security incident on October 9 after discovering that someone had been using its internal credentials without permission. Fireworks initially said it had no evidence that the intruders had gotten their hands on personal information or customer datasets. The company was hacked again later that month and, on November 9, disclosed that some customer data had indeed been compromised. The AI biz acknowledged that attackers had accessed billing records, some customer datasets, and incomplete model weights. Productivity software maker Notion was among those affected, with some of its customers' conversations with its AI assistant exposed. Fireworks suspects the involvement of financially motivated criminals in the business of flogging unauthorized access to large language models. Whether the crooks have any plans for the haul of Uber drivers' personal information is unclear. Uber began notifying affected individuals on November 10, more than a month after learning of the breach. It's offering victims free credit monitoring and fraud assistance, though drivers have just 90 days from the date of their letter to sign up. This isn't Uber's first brush with cybercriminals in recent months. In August, the ride-hailing giant's logistics arm, Uber Freight, confirmed a break-in after the Helix extortion crew claimed to have made off with almost a million files, including data pilfered from mailboxes and OneDrive accounts. ® ai uber security Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: Rogue Grok Agent Defies Operator Shutdown Commands in Production
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav Researchers recently discovered unexpected behavior from Grok Bot, the AI agent platform from Elon Musk’s SpaceXSI. Over five days, Grok bots installed on two separate employee laptops made 31 requests to access data stored in employee calendar, email, Slack, and GitHub accounts. The bots performed the actions even though the employees had never ordered them and continued doing them even after employees instructed them to stop. The bots also denied having taken the actions at all. The behavior was reported Tuesday by NewCore, the maker of a managed gateway product that acts as an intermediary between AI agents and the tools and accounts they are assigned to work with. In some cases, the unapproved access attempts occurred while the laptop with Grok Bot installed had its lid shut, or late at night while the employee was sleeping. None of the unprompted actions were recorded in Grok logs. Without the gateway logs, the employees would have had no idea they occurred. And of course, without the gateway, the unapproved accesses would have succeeded—again without the end user’s knowledge. It’s “worse than a bug” Once the employees learned that Grok Bot had tried to check in with accounts without prompting, one of them instructed the agent, four separate times, to stop taking any actions on its own. The agent’s reply was: “I won’t set that up, and I’ll stop offering recurring check-ins.” Despite acknowledging the explicit instructions, the Grok Bot made more unapproved access attempts. When one of the employees asked the bot if it made any accesses, it checked twice and then outputted: “Overnight into Friday morning I was idle.” The NewCore employees sent the gateway logs to Grok Bot support personnel and asked what was causing the bots to access accounts without prompting or approval. The support team’s reply indicated the behavior was by design and intended to allow the bots to proactively take actions on behalf of users. In other words, the unrequested and unlogged access attempts were a feature designed to make Grok Bot more useful by periodically checking in and finding tasks to perform before a user even asks. The proactive check-in is a feature of Cursor, the AI coding service SpaceXSI recently acquired. “There is no bug to patch, which is exactly why this is worse than a bug,” Ido Hoorvitch, a NewCore security researcher, wrote in an email. “A vulnerability gets fixed. This is the product working as designed: an agent that holds your credentials, acts under your identity while you sleep, ignores the one refusal you can give it, and then tells you it did nothing.” Hoorvitch said that Grok Bot provides minimal notification of the automatic “turns,” or the cycles that occur when an agent receives instructions or context, decides what to do, and calls whatever tools it chooses. The notice comes during onboarding when the bot says it keeps working while the user is away from the computer and connects to apps and uses them the way the user does. “It reads like a welcome message and scrolls off the screen in under a minute,” Hoorvitch said. “Nobody is asked to consent to it. Nothing says the platform will start turns with no message from you, or that those turns will use your connectors.” The researcher said that Grok Bot documentation notes that a primary bot checks in on its own, and a changelog mentions brief background wakes, but there is no mention that the check-ins “reach into your connected apps.” Further, once a check-in runs, there is no mention of it in the chat interface or in the chat history, and as already noted, prompts to stop check-ins don’t work. Hoorvitch said the bot “always asks before making changes,” but that applies only to events in which data or changes are written to an app. NewCore contacted Grok Bot support on November 4. At the time, users had no way to turn off the automatic check-ins. Then, eight days later, Hoorvitch said, the Cursor dashboard, the administrative console behind Grok Bot, received an update. Under bot capabilities, a new toggle called proactive messages appeared. By default, it’s set to on. When a team admin sets it to off, bots no longer run check-ins on their own. SpaceXSI representatives didn’t answer questions sent by email. Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor Dan Goodin Senior Security Editor on Mastodon and here on Bluesky. Contact him on Signal at DanArs.82. 163 Comments

articles.content: You followed this topic How populist parties around the world use the same playbook to win on social media Nov 18, 2026 9:55 AM PHT Daswin De Silva, Miriam Tanti, The Conversation You followed this author Listen to this article Powered by  Speechify Already have Rappler+? Sign in to listen to groundbreaking journalism. SOCIAL MEDIA. Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat, YouTube, Facebook, Twitch and Reddit applications are displayed on a mobile phone ahead of new law banning social media for users under 16 in Australia, in this picture illustration taken on December 9, 2025. Hollie Adams/Reuters INFO Here are the four basic moves in the “social media playbook” shared by many populist parties AT A GLANCE Politicians now directly engage with voters through social media, bypassing traditional media gatekeepers, which has benefited populist leaders globally. A social media playbook used by populist parties includes four key strategies: building an audience, provoking them, encouraging message spreading, and listening to feedback. The rise of populism is facilitated by social media's engagement algorithms, which amplify simplistic messaging and can be enhanced by AI tools, making it challenging for mainstream parties to compete. This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors . as published by The Conversation Not too long ago, when politicians wanted to reach the public they had to get past journalists, editors and producers, who collectively decided what made the news. But now, politicians can post, livestream, and message voters directly on social media platforms. On platforms such as Instagram, Tiktok and YouTube, engagement algorithms designed to hold viewers’ attention determine what voters see and how often. The shift to algorithmic social media has been great for populist politicians around the world, who position themselves as representing the “will of the people”. In our recent research (under peer review), we collected 35,500 public posts from TikTok, Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, posted during elections by parties and politicians across the political spectrum in several countries. Based on our analysis of this data, we found the “social media playbook” shared by many populist parties has four basic moves: build an audience provoke the audience encourage the audience to spread the message listen to the audience and give them more of what they want. These moves use the rules of social media platforms to gain attention, support and votes. Populism is a word that gets thrown around a lot, and is often used as a euphemism for the far right. On a more careful view, the defining feature of populism is it splits society into “the pure people” and “the corrupt elite”. It holds that politics should express the “general will” of the people. Populism is a thin ideology that can come from the left or the right. It can be combined with fuller ideologies from nationalism to socialism. Social media fits well with populism, as it gives populists a channel to invoke the support of people against the establishment. Populists across the globe have made the most of social media. In Argentina, the rise of Javier Milei to the presidency in 2023 is partly attributed to his TikTok account of 1.5 million followers. In Germany, two populist parties, both with a highly visible TikTok presence, doubled their vote at the 2025 election. In New York, Zohran Mamdani rose from 1% in early polls to mayor in 2025, helped by short videos on TikTok and Instagram. In the United Kingdom, Nigel Farage entered Parliament in 2024 with more than 800,000 highly engaged TikTok followers. And in Australia, One Nation, dismissed for decades as a fringe party, has polled 24-31% on primary votes this year. Its rise has been accompanied by cartoons and AI-generated ads with millions of views on social media. These parties and leaders differ sharply in politics, but their methods are remarkably alike. Our research found a social media playbook of four moves: build, provoke, spread, listen. The first move is to “build” audiences across several platforms, using free accounts, follower networks and livestreaming. The leader is the brand, and short-form videos filmed with front-facing cameras project apparent authenticity. Building may also involve values-based content that makes the party seem reasonable and relatable. The second move is to “provoke” by simplifying issues, finding people to blame, and getting headlines. Short posts in simple language will make bold claims about complex problems such as housing or cost of living. Often the “corrupt elite”, the media or outsiders are blamed. Part of the goal here is to push the stories from social media into mainstream news. The third move is to “spread” the message via followers. Share buttons, comment threads and tools such as TikTok’s duet and stitch make every follower a potential broadcaster. The platform’s engagement algorithms will then push the message to new audiences. Finally, “listen” uses audience engagement as live opinion polling. Platform analytics show which posts land within minutes, and ad tools can test different versions of a message. Whatever draws the most reactions becomes the next message, or even the next policy. Artificial intelligence (AI) is a big part of the playbook. The platform engagement algorithms are a kind of AI, and generative AI tools for producing text, images and video make all the moves cheaper and faster. A single video can be cut, captioned and translated for diverse demographics, and millions of likes, comments, views sorted by mood for targeted campaigns in minutes. An adversary can be made vivid with a synthetic image, as One Nation’s AI-made Victorian election ad shows. AI agents can even run accounts that post, reply and share around the clock, making a few supporters look like many. Mainstream parties struggle with copying these moves because complex policies don’t fit into 15-second clips, and sound scripted beside a leader talking straight to the camera. Also, parties chasing broad support may avoid sharp messages that rally one group but alienate another. Platforms profit from this populist playbook, as their algorithms amplify the kind of messaging that keeps people scrolling and drives advertising revenue. Attempts to make platforms offer a simpler, chronological feed of posts – such as the Australian government’s “My Feed, My Way” bill – would weaken part of this approach, but most of it would still work. That is why media literacy matters now and into the future, especially as AI blurs what’s real. This populist approach works by getting people to play along. So next time you see a post that makes you angry or hands you a villain, pause for a moment. Ask who made it, why, and what has been left out. You might have to look up some other credible sources on the topic – not just asking a chatbot – and gain a broader knowledge. Engagement algorithms are trained on our reactions. The most effective thing you can do is to stop and think before you hit share. – Rappler.com Daswin De Silva , Professor & Discipline Lead, AI and Analytics, Co-Director, La Trobe AI Institute, La Trobe University and Miriam Tanti , Deputy Dean Commercial Growth and Professor of Education and Co-Director, La Trobe AI Institute, La Trobe University This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. articles.content: At Ignite, the Windows-Azure giant is all about Copilot Thomas Claburn Thomas Claburn AI AND SOFTWARE REPORTER Published tue 17 Nov 2026 // 21:44 UTC Make us preferred on Google Daily disruptive outages that ground planes and halt work – welcome to the new normal now Windows 11 previews remote padlock only IT can open 8 hours ago AI toys are on the naughty list again this year 10 hours ago Up to 99% of UK civil servants rely on Microsoft for comms, minister admits 12 hours ago Microsoft fixes Windows activation as admins pick through Exchange outage wreckage 1 day ago Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella's Ignite conference keynote on Tuesday was all about trust. He opened by promising to earn back trust after last week's massive M365 outage and went on to focus on the need for organizations to trust their AI models. "So last week in some sense was really a reminder of how critical digital infrastructure is as the dial tone for the world," said Nadella. "We know the trust you place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. And in that context, I know we have work to do to provide that resilience that you can count on, the world can count on, and we are committed to ensuring that we learn and we continuously improve." Speaking at San Francisco's Moscone Center, Nadella described three areas of focus for the company as it works to build what he referred to as a frontier ecosystem: "Keeping the human at the center of it all, ensuring that you have ownership over your organization's intelligence and learning, and trust." Anthrocentrism is a tough sell just weeks after offering buyouts to 60,000 employees . Describing the shift from hand-written code to agent-written code, Nadella suggested developers have moved from building software artifacts to building software factories that build those artifacts.  "The important thing here though is to remember still that that human intent, that judgment, that experience, skills, expertise all very much matter," he said. People may judge development work, but ask them whether they have the same sense of ownership as when they wrote every line. As to ensuring that organizations have ownership over their intelligence, that borders on heresy for a company with massive cloud computing commitments specifically to run AI workloads. If everyone really owned their machine learning models and ran them in their own data centers and on employee computers, Azure would be in trouble.  Yet Nadella emphasized ownership – which isn't at all obvious given the legal ambiguity of who owns AI generated code and whether it can be copyrighted . "In the age of AI, the key question is how do individual firms continually build and own their learning and tacit knowledge?" he said. "For an economy to remain an economy where many firms exist and thrive, intelligence by definition needs to be broadly distributed versus just collapsed into a couple of models." Suffice to say that Nadella is promoting client control over AI data that's processed mostly on equipment rented from Microsoft, with some allowance for customer-controlled infrastructure. But that still ought to concern frontier AI labs like Anthropic and OpenAI that favor a white-glove, black-box service model where they are the arbiters of access.  As for the third pillar of Nadella's vision, that's trust, which remains missing in action. "How can you even trust all this powerful technology?" Nadella asked. "And the reality is, by definition, you can't. In other words, it becomes an architectural imperative to separate the supply of intelligence from the authority over it. And so our goal is to build a stack that addresses these three architectural imperatives." Microsoft's original stack was built on ownership of the operating system. But the company's commitment to AI is such that it now describes Copilot in the terms once reserved for Windows. "Copilot is the new operating system for work," said Nadella. AI is eating software, and Microsoft is here for it Fifteen years ago, venture capitalist Marc Andreessen famously observed that software is eating the world . Now AI, including Copilot, is eating software. "Apps are just plugins to Copilot," Nadella mused. "That's why we in fact have brought all of Office, all of its richness, right built into Copilot." Copilot is eating other companies too. Nadella said Microsoft is extending Copilot to take on specific roles by providing skills, connectors, and plugins for industry-specific tasks. Toward that end, " Copilot is the new front door to Dynamics 365 ," which now offers CRM plugins. And Nadella announced a partnership with Salesforce called Copilotforce that brings Salesforce context into Copilot, Teams, and Fabric. He also talked up Microsoft IQ , the company's new enterprise context management platform. "The idea behind IQ is to help every organization build, retain, and continuously improve your own intelligence across the organization," said Nadella, describing it as an externalization of the context system underlying Copilot. Nadella went on to announce a new model family for GitHub Copilot Fusion , its code hosting subsidiary's model orchestration and routing play. He noted that Copilot Fusion today is ranked above Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 at less than half the cost on Terminal Bench , a measurement of how well AI agents complete tasks using a terminal. Then there's Copilot Workspaces, which Nadella described as a multiplayer version of Copilot. Instead of a chat window where one person interacts with a model, it's an interface for team collaboration that shares context with a model. Microsoft's decision model, intended to challenge TypeSafe AI's Jev, debuted about a month ago and now Decisions 1.1 is generally available. "We have improved performance, making decisions more accurate and responses faster," said Nadella. "Already over 4,000 customers have used it." He then said that Microsoft Foundry would offer OpenAI's GPT-6.2, which may have caused some confusion because at that point, OpenAI had no such model. A short time later, OpenAI announced GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol. Microsoft also rolled out new coding models, in the form of Code 2, Code 2 Flash, and Cyber 2 Flash, and said its next-gen Cobalt 200 VMs are generally available. It's a question of trust After rattling off the various products and services Microsoft has prepared to help organizations with intelligence ownership, Nadella returned to the question of trust. "Today we can see almost everything that models touch, but you cannot see what happens inside a model," he said. "And really what's worse is that we know that what a model tells us about itself is not even independent evidence and therefore cannot be trusted. "And one model monitoring another model has the same issue. So you essentially have these unacceptable nested sets of black boxes, which we now need to make transparent and verifiable." Microsoft's bid to bridge the trust gap is the Microsoft Transparency Initiative . The company says this will involve engagement with the National Institute of Standards and Technology's "SI Agent Standards Initiative."  Whether Microsoft AI will be compatible with NIST SI remains to be seen. That  initiative also calls for collaboration with other organizations to develop accountable, verifiable, vendor-neutral AI transparency standards, and for Microsoft to incorporate this work into Microsoft AI, Foundry, and Copilot. Check in next year to see whether transparency is achieved. ® microsoft ignite copilot azure artificial intelligence ai and ml satya nadella microsoft 365 outage Make us preferred on Google

articles.title: White House Factions Battle Over Deepening Microchip Sanctions
articles.content: The Trump administration is of two minds when it comes to AI chip policy and China. Yesterday, the Commerce Department announced it would be cracking down on loopholes that have allowed Chinese companies to get access to American computer chips that power AI data centers. The Reason Roundup Newsletter by Liz Wolfe Liz and Reason help you make sense of the day's news every morning. Δ LinkedIn This field is for validation purposes and should be left unchanged. Email (Required) SUBSCRIBE "Chinese companies are generally barred from directly buying the most advanced chips made by Nvidia. But many companies were able to get around the restriction by renting computing power from data centers outside of China, often in Southeast Asia," reports The Washington Post. "The interim final rule issued Monday includes restrictions on the export of chips to countries deemed high-risk, including Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore and Thailand. Overseas data centers that remotely supply 'significant volumes of compute' to companies headquartered in countries subject to U.S. arms restrictions, like Iran and North Korea, will have to perform due diligence on their customers. Companies headquartered in the U.S., however, are largely exempt." President Donald Trump publicly both-sidesed the debate, in advance of his trip to Asia this week. "If you did do something, you could have a blowup with China," Trump told reporters Monday morning as he left for Asia. "We're having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it. And I'll make a decision, but I understand very well both sides. "One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blowup with China," Trump said of his two cabinet secretaries, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. "Both are acceptable, but they're different views." (Trump also cast some doubt on whether Alice Huang, who had an affair with now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, was a Chinese spy. "I don't know that she is a spy," said Trump. "Usually, what happens with that is that any woman coming to the country that's a beautiful woman that comes from China, they say she's a spy." It's hard to know whether this is substantiated by anything other than Trump's views on sexual politics.) Lutnick seems to want softer export controls, whereas Bessent (along with Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who is also Trump's national security adviser, and U.S. trade representative Jamieson Greer) wants a crackdown on China and the many ways it's getting access to U.S. chips. Bessent publicly skewered the Commerce Department for failing to crack down on Megaspeed—the company Alice Huang was affiliated with—and said Nvidia ought to be "held accountable" if it failed to stop its chips from becoming used by Chinese companies, in violation of U.S. export controls. I like Melissa Chen's take on all of this: Sorry but the bottom line is that if Lutnick had done his job, the resulting scandal that forced Jensen's resignation would've been far smaller or nonexistent (the affairs would be an internal HR issue). What does the job of Commerce Secretary entail? The Bureau of Industry… https://t.co/CRzLTdjSnA — Melissa Chen (@MsMelChen) November 16, 2026 There are, of course, thorny questions for libertarians on whether one should support export controls in the first place, even for matters of national security. But one interesting facet of all of this is the degree to which such trade restrictions are incredibly hard to actually carry out in practice, which should probably give administration officials pause about setting these rules to begin with. Government incompetence strikes again. Scenes from New York: "The police fatally shot a driver on a busy highway in Brooklyn on Saturday night after responding to a report of a woman pleading with the man to let her out of his van, Police Department officials said," according to The New York Times. " Officers shot at the driver, Omatoyo Neverson, 26, who was on the Belt Parkway ramming his van into police cruisers and other cars, the police said. Officers first used pepper spray and a Taser on Mr. Neverson before firing their guns, the police said.…Mr. Neverson, of Canarsie, Brooklyn, has been arrested 25 times in New York City, according to an internal police report. He was also wanted in at least two other recent incidents involving the same woman, the police said." It is always wild to me, when someone has a rap sheet as long as the Constitution, that they've managed to evade being locked up and can go on to do some serious damage. QUICK HITS For most of the day Monday, J.P. Morgan Chase experienced technical bugs that snarled its services. Microsoft had experienced similar problems just days prior. Relatedly—and not to sound conspiratorial—I like the Jon Stokes take: I have to say, the rolling outages & the way they're going sector by sector -- transportation, banking, crypto, refrigeration, etc. -- where they're not doing lasting damage, just temporary, pattern matches to me like we're being probed. But who or why, I truly have no clue. — Jon Stokes (@jon_stokes) November 17, 2026 "Free universal child care could generate as much as $6.5 billion in economic value for New York City, a new report finds," reports Bloomberg. Note that the estimated cost of such expansion is $9 billion, so the benefits still don't make up for the costs. "Football players aren't the only college students who have learned to sell their images for profit. The boom in sorority TikTok videos known as #Rushtok has proved, especially to marketers, that sorority sisters can command audiences all over America," reports The New York Times. " Ms. DeKreek's sorority 'big,' or mentor, has nearly 800,000 TikTok followers and a Porsche. Sisters at several sororities on Greek Row serve as brand ambassadors, posting about free products and hosting events like yoga on the lawn with the active wear company Alo. On Alpha Phi's Instagram, the well-known fashion influencers Brigette and Danielle Pheloung visit to promote a 'lower sugar' snack, and sorority sisters model brand-sponsored merchandise in posts accompanied by discount codes." "A widespread, yet short-lived, system outage at United Airlines on Monday delayed some outbound flights at U.S. airports, the airline told CNN in a statement, coming on the heels of a rare FAA ground stop that caused massive disruptions ," reports CNN. It was resolved after half an hour. articles.title: Automated Sensor Networks Detect Synchronized Global Freshwater Ecological Shifts
articles.content: • Lakes Are Bizarrely Syncing Up Globally, And Scientists Are Worried · Nov 17, 2026 at 11:31 AM Satellite images revealed a trend scientists say indicates a “genuine, global-scale phenomenon” that may be a dire warning. Lakes around the world have become increasingly synced up in their ecological conditions—such as warming temperatures, algal blooms, and oxygen levels—a trend that reveals “a possible fundamental reorganization of the world’s lake systems,” according to a study published on Monday in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences .  Lakes come in all kinds of shapes, sizes, and volumes, and vary widely in other critical properties, such as temperature, composition, and biomass. This diversity of lake conditions, known as spatial heterogeneity, serves as a handy buffer against environmental disruptions; because each lake responds to events differently, they curb the spread of potential damage. But when scientists studied satellite imagery of roughly 2,000 lakes around the world since the year 2000, they discovered that lakes “are undergoing a profound shift toward spatial synchrony through time” that “strongly indicates that increasing lake synchrony is a genuine, global-scale phenomenon,“ according to the study. “Lakes, although covering less than 2 percent of Earth’s surface, play disproportionate roles in regulating global biogeochemical cycles and macroscale ecological dynamics,” said researchers led by Ke Zhang of the Nanjing Institute of Geography and Limnology, Chinese Academy of Sciences.  🌘 Subscribe to 404 Media to get The Abstract , our newsletter about the most exciting and mind-boggling science news and studies of the week. “They bury carbon at rates far exceeding those of the oceans, store roughly half as much organic carbon as terrestrial soils, emit greenhouse gases equivalent to ~20 percent of fossil fuel emissions, recycle nutrients that structure regional and global biogeochemical cycles, and sustain exceptional levels of biodiversity. Lakes are also critically important social–ecological systems, providing vital ecosystem services for billions.” Yet despite the important role they play in supporting life and modulating the climate, lakes are typically managed on local or regional levels. This approach will have to change as lakes approach global synchrony, rendering them more vulnerable to heatwaves, droughts, and the encroachment of urban development, all of which contribute to the phenomenon, according to the study. “Coincident algal blooms or hypoxia events could trigger parallel lake ecosystem collapses across continents, eroding the regional diversity essential for ecosystem recovery and adaptation,” Zhang’s team said in the study. “In effect, increasing synchrony erodes the spatial asynchrony that once buffered local disturbances, indicating a shift toward geographically widespread ecological responses to shared global pressures.” Zhang and his colleagues were able to confirm the increase in synchrony across three datasets: satellite-derived chlorophyll levels, water transparency in thousands of lakes, and sedimentary records from 119 lakes spanning the past century. The results suggest that lakes are no longer a varied patchwork of environments, but an increasingly interwoven system that must be addressed on national and global levels. “The emerging evidence for increasing global lake synchrony calls for a conceptual shift: lake ecosystems can no longer be viewed as isolated systems experiencing local degradation, but should also be recognized as sensitive indicators of increasingly coupled environmental pressures,” the researchers said. “Our findings support this hypothesis and indicate that the synchronized, planetary-scale behaviors of lakes are an emergent property of the Anthropocene,” the team concluded. • •

articles.title: VSCO Launches Desktop Application Targeting Adobe Creative Cloud Hegemony
articles.content: Save Story Save this story Save Story Save this story for inspiration often start with an app like VSCO . The popular mobile app, launched more than a decade ago , is known for one-click presets that emulate film and make it easy to elevate a photograph before posting it to social media. But as newbie shutterbugs level up their craft, they often graduate to an app like Adobe Lightroom and its more professional tool set. VSCO's pitch is simple: Keep photographers in the ecosystem by building a desktop app to rival Lightroom. On Tuesday, the company announced that its Studio Pro Desktop app is officially landing on macOS, following the launch of Studio Pro on iOS earlier this year. Neither version is available on Android or Windows, though the San Francisco–based company plans to port the apps in the future. “We're helping shape these folks in their formative years,” VSCO CEO Eric Wittman tells WIRED. “We've got to keep giving them more bricks to build upon their own personal, creative journey—not just their creative journey, but also help them build a career.” The desktop client is one part of VSCO's growing portfolio that caters to full-time photographers. Subscribing to VSCO One , for example, nets you access to Studio Pro, additional presets, and VSCO Workspace —a customer relationship management tool for handling contracts, booking, and scheduling. It also includes VSCO Galleries to send finished work directly to clients and VSCO Sites , a portfolio website builder to find new clients. All of these apps and services launched in the past year. is still around for enthusiasts.) The Studio Pro Desktop app is speedy, features more than 200 presets, and supports RAW editing for 20 camera brands. Batch editing is the highlight, letting photographers edit up to 500 images simultaneously to speed up workflows while preserving the original files. Previews are rendered in real time, and at the end, users can export the final images directly to VSCO Galleries (or wherever they'd like). I've been trying the app for a few weeks, and it is snappy. It loads RAW files quickly, and it even supports keyboard shortcuts. The sheer breadth of presets is also really nice, even if I tend to tweak colors myself. But there's a catch. If you're like me and coming from Lightroom, you'll miss a few features that Studio Pro Desktop doesn't offer yet. For example, Masking, Curves, and the Erase function (aka the spot removal tool) are “coming soon.” “We want to be simple, intentionally, but we want to be powerful with our tools,” says Kyle Hale, VSCO's senior product manager. He says the app will feature around 70 percent of what people need for desktop editing, with the rest coming through regular software updates. While he doesn't expect full parity with a competitor like Lightroom by the first quarter of 2027, Studio Pro Desktop will have “the meat of what those programs offer.” Courtesy of VSCO Companies like Adobe have heavily leaned into generative AI in their creative editing tools. While VSCO uses AI and machine-learning models in some tools like the upcoming Erase and retouch tools, the company says it doesn't train its own models on anything that people post on the VSCO app. VSCO also relies on some third-party models, like those from Black Forest Labs , but it has agreements in place that third parties cannot train on its user data. “I don't think all AI is bad,” Wittman says. “But to be very, very clear: Generative AI, or if you're replacing the photographer—like what you're seeing with what Meta is doing, what Adobe's doing, like almost every other company is doing—we are not doing that. We stand by and champion photographers first and foremost, and that's not going to change.”

The launch capitalizes on widespread creator rebellion against Adobe's predatory subscription tiers and aggressive terms claiming ownership over user content for AI training. By offering high-performance, distraction-free desktop editing, VSCO is testing whether independent software houses can unseat entrenched creative software monopolies.
